subject: Accounting
title: Bad Debts and Write-Offs
description: Learn Bad Debts and Write-Offs in one minute.

hook.text: A customer declares bankruptcy. The $10,000 they owe you is never coming. Now what?

buildup.text: Bad debt expense recognizes that some receivables will never be collected.

discovery.text: Companies estimate bad debts using historical rates or aging analysis and create an allowance account.

twist.text: Writing off a receivable doesn't mean giving up—you can still pursue legal action to collect.

climax.text: Proper bad debt accounting keeps receivable balances honest and prevents overstated assets.

punchline.text: Not every customer pays. Plan for it.

quiz.question: Why do companies estimate bad debts?

details.summary: Bad debts are receivables that a business determines it cannot collect. This topic covers the allowance method vs. direct write-off method, how to estimate uncollectible amounts, and the impact of bad debts on financial statements.
details.whyItMatters: Every business that extends credit will eventually face customers who don't pay. Properly accounting for bad debts prevents overstating assets and provides a realistic picture of financial health.
takeaways: The allowance method estimates bad debts before they occur, matching expense to revenue period
The direct write-off method records bad debt only when a specific account is deemed uncollectible
GAAP requires the allowance method for most businesses because it better matches expenses to revenue

faq.question: What is the difference between the allowance method and direct write-off method?
faq.answer: The allowance method estimates bad debts in advance and records an expense each period, while the direct write-off method records the loss only when a specific customer is confirmed uncollectible. GAAP prefers the allowance method for better matching.

faq.question: How do businesses estimate bad debts?
faq.answer: Common methods include percentage of sales (applying a historical rate to credit sales) and aging of receivables (applying increasing percentages to older unpaid invoices). Both use past experience to predict future uncollectible amounts.
